newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia bishops blame "moral decay" for violence.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia bishops blame "moral decay" for violence.

text.p: Indonesian Catholic bishops on Sunday blamed recent riots in the mainly Moslem country on "moral decay in almost all aspects of life".
"...The law is disregarded, people's basic rights are not respected...this decay can threaten the nation's unity and future," the Indonesian Bishops' Conference said in a statement.

On Thursday, rioters set fire to a church and a Chinese Buddhist temple, wrecked four other churches and looted shops and homes in Rengasdengklok, 50 kilometres (30 miles) east of Jakarta, over reports that an ethnic Chinese woman had insulted Moslems. Sixteen cars were also destroyed.

In December, four people were killed when a mob went on a rampage in the town of Tasikmalaya, about 200 km (125 miles) south-east of Jakarta. Rioters, angered by reports of police brutality towards a Moslem religious teacher, set fire to shops, buildings and churches.
The bishops said in the statement that they had urged Catholics not to become alarmed over the incidents. The statement gave no other details.

Government officials said the Rengasdengklok riot apparently started after a Chinese woman complained of the noise Moslem youths made as they beat drums before dawn to summon people to eat before the start of the daylight Ramadan fast.
Newspapers reported police have arrested 20 people, including the Chinese woman and her husband, on charges of destruction of property and looting.
Ethnic Chinese, some of whom are Christians, are often resented for their relative affluence compared to ethnic Malays and are frequently the targets of mob violence in Indonesia.

About 80 percent of Indonesia's 200 million people are Moslems, making it the world's most populous Moslem nation. Other religions recognised by the government are Catholicism Protestantism, Hinduism and Buddhism.

Political and social analysts have blamed the eruptions of violence on socio-economic tensions. Some government members have said they believed a Maoist conspiracy was involved but have provided no proof.
